prompt.context: Our client is the third largest greeting card company in the US. Revenue has been increasing 1-2% per year, but profits have been declining at about 5% per year over the past 2-3 years. The new CEO wants to know why.
prompt.question: Why are profits declining despite growing revenue, and what can the company do to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.q: Is there differentiation between greeting card products?
clarifying_info.a: There is no real differentiation between greeting card products. Stores will not recognize differentiated products.
Cards are distributed through card shops, mass retailers, and miscellaneous other shops. These stores choose only one source for their greeting cards.

clarifying_info.q: What is our client's market share?
clarifying_info.a: Our client has a 25% share. Number 1 and 2 competitors have 35% and 30%.
The market is growing 3-4% per year, and market shares are stable.
Fixed costs are up 1% per year in line with wage rate and inflationary increases. Variable costs are flat.

The price per card is basically the same across all card types. The price printed on the cards (suggested retail price) is increased 5% per year. Typically the company sells to retailers for a discount off the suggested retail price.

exhibits.title: Sales by Distribution Channel
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing the breakdown of sales across distribution channels: mass retailers, card shops, and miscellaneous other shops.

framework: Fixed costs: up 1%/yr (wage & inflation) — not a major driver
Variable costs: flat — not a driver
Revenue: price x quantity; SRP up 5%/yr, volume up — but actual revenue only up 1-2%, implying net price to client is falling
Product mix: unchanged — not a driver
Distribution channels: discounts vary by channel; channel mix may be shifting
Key insight: investigate discount structure and channel mix shift as root cause of margin compression

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — Costs and Revenue: Walk through the P&L to isolate the source of declining profits.
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies that with volume up, SRP up 5%, variable costs flat, and fixed costs up only 1%, the math only works if actual realized price (net of discounts) is falling. The candidate should zero in on discounts given to stores as the only remaining explanation.

math.setup: Revenue up 1-2% yet SRP up 5% and volume up. Fixed costs up 1%, variable costs flat. Profits down 5%.
steps: If SRP +5% and volume up, gross revenue should rise well above 1-2%
Fixed cost +1% on a rising revenue base is dilutive but small
Variable costs flat means no cost inflation there
The gap between expected revenue growth (~5%+) and actual revenue growth (~1-2%) must come from larger discounts to distribution channels
math.answer: Discounts given to retailers must be increasing, squeezing realized revenue and driving the profit decline.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — Distribution Channels: What does the channel breakdown tell us, and what is the key driver of the discount problem?
questions.guidance: The candidate should note that retailers represent 80% of sales and negotiate exclusive deals with increasing discounts. Card shops (10%) and misc (10%) have stable discounts. The growing share of the high-discount retailer channel compounds the problem. Key insight: giving increasing discounts to retailers (the dominant channel) is driving down profits.

math.setup: Discounts by channel: card shops — low/stable; mass retailers — 75% off SRP (and increasing); miscellaneous — 50% off SRP (stable). Channel mix: retailers 80%, card shops 10%, misc 10%.
steps: Retailers = 80% of sales, discount 75% and rising
Blended discount is dominated by the retailer discount
As retailer channel grows and their discount increases, realized revenue per card falls
math.answer: The rising discount to mass retailers (80% of sales) combined with a potentially growing share of retailer sales is the primary driver of profit decline.

brainstorming.prompt: Are there any ways you can think of to increase profits? You can think beyond the discount problem.

categories.name: Market consolidation
ideas: Seek a merger with a competitor — industry consolidation gives a larger firm more market power and pricing leverage with retailers

categories.name: Vertical integration
ideas: Vertically integrate (e.g., own printing/manufacturing) to reduce variable costs and improve margins

categories.name: Product/channel expansion
ideas: Expand into complementary products such as teddy bears and balloons — must be products that leverage the existing distribution network
Explore opening or acquiring more company-owned card shops to reduce dependence on mass retailers and their aggressive discounts

recommendation: The root cause of declining profits is the increasing discounts given to mass retailers, who represent 80% of sales, combined with stable or growing retailer channel share — this has eroded realized revenue per card even as volume and SRP grew

To reverse the trend, the company should: (1) renegotiate retailer discount terms or introduce tiered volume-based incentives, (2) explore industry consolidation via merger to gain bargaining power, (3) vertically integrate to cut costs, and (4) expand into adjacent products (teddy bears, balloons) that can travel through the existing distribution network
risks: Retailers may respond to discount renegotiation by switching to a competitor, given no product differentiation
Merger execution risk and regulatory scrutiny in a concentrated market
Adjacent product expansion requires new competencies and may dilute focus
next_steps: Analyze contract terms with top retailer accounts to identify renegotiation opportunities
Benchmark competitor discount structures to assess room to push back
Evaluate M&A targets and synergy potential among top 3 players
Pilot complementary product lines in owned card shops to test demand
